title: What a Heat Pump Really Costs to Install, and What Help Is Left

scenes.purpose: Put the viewer at the kitchen table with two quotes.

visual.description: Warm dark field; "The quotes land on the kitchen table" settles in large type as the sentence begins.
onScreenText: The quotes land on the kitchen table

scenes.narration: Say your furnace gives out in January, and the quotes land on the kitchen table: a new furnace, or a heat pump, and the heat pump is the bigger number.

scenes.purpose: Pose the first question.

visual.description: The question types on, centred; "different jobs" turns amber as it is spoken.
onScreenText: The real price gap, or different jobs?

scenes.narration: Is that the real price gap, or are the quotes pricing different jobs?

scenes.purpose: Pose the second question.

visual.description: The question types on, centred; "still there" turns amber as it is spoken.
onScreenText: Is the federal heat pump money still there?

scenes.narration: And once you know the price, is any of the federal heat pump money you have heard about still there to help?

scenes.purpose: Give the usual view in the channel's own words.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "the most expensive" turns red as it is spoken.
onScreenText: "for upfront cost the furnace is going to be the cheapest the heat pump is going to be the most expensive"

scenes.narration: The channel Atlas AC puts the usual view plainly: "for upfront cost the furnace is going to be the cheapest the heat pump is going to be the most expensive".

scenes.purpose: Give the opposite claim in its own words.

visual.description: Quote card, text only, mirrored from the previous one; "costs less" turns green as it is spoken.
onScreenText: "Installing a heat pump often costs less than simply swapping in a new AC and furnace or boiler"

scenes.narration: EnergySage says nearly the opposite: "Installing a heat pump often costs less than simply swapping in a new AC and furnace or boiler".

scenes.purpose: Name the two baselines the rest of the question compares against.

visual.description: Two lines build one under the other as they are spoken: the furnace on its own, then the furnace plus the air conditioner.
onScreenText: A furnace plus the air conditioner

scenes.direction: Build each line on its words; hold 1 s.
scenes.narration: The difference is what you compare the heat pump with: a furnace on its own, or a furnace plus the air conditioner beside it.

scenes.purpose: Against a furnace alone, the heat pump costs more.

visual.description: Two tiles: the $3,000 average gap in the HVAC database, then the $6,600 average extra cost of switching to a heat pump.

chart.title: Heat pump vs. a furnace alone

points.label: Fuel-fired heating averaged less than heat pumps by
Average extra cost of a heat pump over a like-for-like heater

chart.note: Two different studies and baselines; the tiles are not a range.

scenes.direction: Tile one on s07, tile two on s08.
scenes.narration: Start with the furnace alone: in one database of recorded HVAC jobs, traditional fuel-fired heating systems averaged $3,000 less than heat pump installations, though a heat pump also does the cooling. Another analysis put the extra cost of replacing a house's existing heater with a heat pump, rather than with the same kind of heater, at an average of $6,600.

scenes.purpose: Turn to the second baseline.

visual.description: Split field: the furnace side slides over to make room for the air conditioner side.

scenes.narration: Now count the air conditioner.

scenes.purpose: Against furnace plus central air, the heat pump is about even.

visual.description: Two tiles side by side: heat pump median installed cost, gas furnace plus central air median; the heat pump tile lands slightly lower.

chart.title: Median installed cost
chart.note: Medians from one study; most of their price ranges overlap.

scenes.narration: One study's median installed costs put a heat pump at $6,185, just $270 below a gas furnace with central air, and most of their price ranges overlap.

scenes.purpose: The electric premium is the cost of adding cooling.

visual.description: Three tiles: all-electric upgrade, gas upgrade, then the cost of adding cooling alone, which lands under the gap.

chart.title: Model projects, homes without cooling
chart.note: Archetypal model projects, including hot water; not measured installs.

scenes.narration: The first database's report points the same way: in its model projects for homes with no cooling, an all-electric heating, cooling and hot-water upgrade cost more than a gas one, but the gap was almost exactly the cost of adding central air on its own.

scenes.purpose: A dissent on upfront price, agreement on lifetime cost.

visual.description: The report passage scrolls in; the higher-upfront-cost phrase is marked.

excerpt.highlight: Despite heat pumps having higher upfront costs

scenes.narration: A Canadian model disagrees on the upfront price: it found heat pumps cost more upfront than gas heating with air conditioning, and come out the lowest-cost option for most households anyway, thanks to their efficiency and doubling as the cooling.

scenes.purpose: The catch: sizing for all the heating.

visual.description: The study passage; the sentence about larger heating loads is marked.

scenes.narration: Another study adds a catch: heat pumps designed to carry all of a home's heating are often more expensive to install than an air conditioner plus gas furnace, because bigger heating loads need bigger heat pumps, new wiring and sometimes panel upgrades.

scenes.purpose: Against an air conditioner alone, the gap is small.

visual.description: Three tiles: the wholesale premium range, then the NREL efficient heat pump and efficient central air costs side by side.

chart.title: Heat pump vs. an air conditioner

points.label: Wholesale premium over a same-size AC

chart.note: Wholesale prices, not installed; the NREL pair is 19 SEER equipment.

scenes.direction: Tile one on s14; the NREL pair on s15.
scenes.narration: If you only need a new air conditioner, the gap shrinks: that study says wholesale heat pumps cost only $200 to $500 more than air conditioners of the same size. A cold-climate report quoting NREL's cost database put an efficient heat pump just $370 above an equally efficient central air conditioner.

scenes.purpose: The dissent: a bigger gap over central air.

visual.description: Two tiles: heat pump median, central air median; the gap is visible.

scenes.narration: The study from earlier disagrees, though: its installed medians put the heat pump about 32 percent above central air alone.

scenes.purpose: Real installs vary with size, type, home and climate.

visual.description: The database passage; the ground-source sentence is marked.

scenes.narration: And real installs spread widely: in the first database, a heat pump's price depended most on its size and type, the home's floor area, the efficiency and the climate zone, and ground-source systems cost far more than other types.

scenes.purpose: The electrical work that can come on top.

visual.description: Three tiles build one per sentence: share of field-test sites needing a new panel, the range of electrical upgrade costs, the typical panel upgrade.

chart.title: The electrical work

points.label: Field-test sites needing a new panel

chart.note: The field test had 21 sites; the panel figure excludes circuit wiring.

citations.label: PNNL 2025, cold-climate heat pump field test (21 sites)

scenes.narration: Then there is the electrical work: in a field test of cold-climate heat pump prototypes at 21 sites, 38 percent needed a new panel. Where electrical upgrades were needed, they alone cost between $3,750 and $8,970 in labour and materials, before the heat pump itself. That was a small test, and a typical panel upgrade on its own is put at $1,954 in the first database's report, plus the wiring for each new dedicated circuit.

scenes.purpose: Answer the first question.

visual.description: Three lines build in turn as they are spoken: costs more, about even, wiring adds.
onScreenText: Against a furnace alone: costs more
Against a furnace and air conditioner: about even
The wiring can add to either

scenes.direction: Build each line on its words; hold 1.5 s.
scenes.narration: So against a furnace alone, a heat pump costs more; against a new furnace and air conditioner together it can come out about even, unless it has to be sized up to carry all the heating, and the wiring can add to either.

scenes.purpose: Turn to the second question.

visual.description: The question types on, centred.
onScreenText: Which tax credits and rebates still exist?

scenes.narration: So what help is left to bring those prices down: which tax credits and rebates still exist?

scenes.purpose: The claim that the credit lasts to 2033.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "through 2033" turns amber as it is spoken.
onScreenText: "technically these heat pump tax credits based on the bill that was signed are available through 2033"

scenes.narration: In an earlier video, The Thought Provocateur told viewers "technically these heat pump tax credits based on the bill that was signed are available through 2033".

scenes.purpose: What the credit was worth.

visual.description: Two tiles: 30 percent of cost, capped at $2,000 a year.

chart.title: Federal heat pump tax credit, from 2023

citations.label: IRS, energy efficient home improvement credit

scenes.narration: That credit was real: from 2023 it was worth 30 percent of the cost of a qualifying heat pump, capped at $2,000 a year.

scenes.purpose: The credit ended with 2025.

visual.description: The IRS table row; the termination date is marked.

scenes.narration: But it was cut short: the IRS says the credit is not allowed for any property placed in service after December 31, 2025, so a heat pump installed after that date cannot claim it.

scenes.purpose: The claim that the rebates survived.

visual.description: Quote card, text only; "survived" turns green as it is spoken.
onScreenText: "the tax credit for heat pumps expired, but the rebate program for heat pumps survived"

scenes.narration: The Rebate Report pointed viewers elsewhere: "the tax credit for heat pumps expired, but the rebate program for heat pumps survived".

scenes.purpose: Who the rebates are for, and states slow to start.

visual.description: The tracker's state entries; the no-launch-date line is marked.

excerpt.highlight: There is currently no expected launch date for Alabama’s rebate programs.

scenes.narration: Those federal rebates, though, were aimed at low- to moderate-income households and run by each state's energy office. And some states were slow to start: in one state-by-state tracker, Alabama, Alaska and Arkansas had their applications only conditionally approved, with no expected launch date.

scenes.purpose: A count of launched programs.

visual.description: Quote card, text only.
onScreenText: "12 states and the District of Columbia"

scenes.narration: Owen Marsh, in a video on what survived, counted "12 states and the District of Columbia" with programs launched as of June.

scenes.purpose: The May 2026 rule change on fuel switching.

visual.description: North Carolina's notice; the fuel-switching line is marked.

excerpt.highlight: Fuel Switching Projects are NOT allowed

scenes.narration: And on May 29, 2026, the Department of Energy changed the rules: the rebate no longer pays to replace gas or other fossil-fuel equipment, only to upgrade existing electric equipment. North Carolina's energy office, for one, says its program had to make the change by September 1, 2026.

scenes.purpose: A generous state program.

visual.description: Three tiles: average install, standard rebate, income-based rebate.

citations.label: Mass Save, air source heat pump rebates

scenes.narration: Some state and utility programs are generous: in Massachusetts, Mass Save's whole-home rebate is $8,500, or $16,000 at the income-based level, against an average install of $22,000 in its 2022 data.

scenes.purpose: The typical rebate is far smaller.

visual.description: Two tiles: median total rebate, and its share of gross project cost.

scenes.narration: But that is one program: in the first database, which predates today's rules, the median total rebate across its projects was $1,327, about 21 percent of gross project cost.

scenes.purpose: Rebates did not close the upfront gap in Canada.

visual.description: The report passage; the rebates phrase is marked.

excerpt.highlight: despite rebates intended to bring down capital costs

scenes.narration: And a Canadian model found heat pumps there still cost more upfront despite rebates meant to bring capital costs down.

scenes.purpose: Answer the second question.

visual.description: Three lines build in turn as they are spoken.
onScreenText: No federal rebate for switching from gas
Rebates trim the price, not erase it

scenes.direction: Build each line on its words; hold 1.5 s.
scenes.narration: So for a heat pump installed in 2026 there is no federal tax credit, the federal rebate no longer covers switching from gas, and where rebates exist, they usually trim the price rather than erase it.

scenes.purpose: What to do before comparing quotes.

visual.description: A short checklist builds one line per sentence.
onScreenText: Decide what you would otherwise buy
Ask about your panel; check rebates before you sign

scenes.direction: Build per sentence; fade out on the last word.
scenes.narration: So before you compare quotes, decide what you would otherwise buy: a furnace alone, or a furnace and an air conditioner. Ask every installer up front whether your panel and service can carry the heat pump, and check your state energy office and your utility for rebates before you sign.
